name: Mário Zagallo
scopeNote: Narrowed on 2026-11-04 (user decision): only the first Brazil spell (1970-74) is counted; the 1995-98 spell is excluded and its sources stay in the file as context with verified false. Zagallo as Brazil head coach in two spells: 1970-1974 (1970 World Cup win, 1974 fourth place) and 1994/95-1998 (1997 Copa America, 1997 Confederations Cup, 1998 World Cup final). The 1970 side is described by sources as a 4-2-4 on paper that played as a fluid/false 4-3-3 with five number tens (Wikipedia: fluid 4-2-3-1, 4-4-1-1 off the ball); the popular label of pure all-out attack is questioned by These Football Times, which says the team was tactically more careful than its myth. The 1998 side is a 4-2-2-2 with a double pivot (Coaches Voice). Excluded spells carry partial dates (years only) because exact days were not found. The 1994 role as technical coordinator under Parreira is excluded (not head coach). Start of spell 1 (16 March 1970) comes from a search summary of Revista Oeste/ESPN (page returned 403) and from FIFA's 75 days before the World Cup; the end dates are approximate (see openQuestions).
openQuestions: Exact start of the 1970 spell: 16 March 1970 comes from a search summary of Revista Oeste citing ESPN (page 403); FIFA says 75 days before the World Cup start (31 May), which computes to about 17 March. Check against a second primary source.
End of spell 1 (1974-07-06) is from memory (date of the third-place match lost to Poland); no digest paragraph gave the day he left the job. Verify.

Start of spell 2: no digest gave the day Zagallo took over from Parreira as head coach; 1995-01-01 is a placeholder year start, not a verified date (sources checked only confirm that he was coordinator in 1994 and head coach in the 1996-97 friendlies and 1997 Copa America). Verify with RSSSF Brasil 1994-95 page or CBF.
End of spell 2 set to the 1998 World Cup final date (1998-07-12); the actual last day in the job was not found. Jovem Pan says only that he left the national team after the Cup.

Coaches Voice says the 1970 team set up in a low 4-4-1-1 block against structured attacks, but also says the back line pushed up to the halfway line when Brazil attacked; the same source says they played a high line. Both are recorded, the contradiction is not resolved.
Wikipedia describes 1970 as fluid 4-2-3-1, FIFA/TFT as 4-2-4 turned into 4-3-3, Coaches Voice as false 4-3-3 with a single pivot (Clodoaldo), Zagallo himself says 4-3-3. Label disagreement.

Decalcanhar (Substack, 2024) argues Zagallo was a conservative coach who did not invent the 4-3-3 and that the 1970 tactical nuance came from the players rather than from Zagallo; TFT 2017 says the joga bonito identity owes more to Saldanha. Contested credit.

Romario cut from the 1998 squad (calf injury, 3 June 1998) and the Copa America 1997 final without Romario appear only in search summaries; not verified in a digest. Relevant to people-management/squad-building and worth a follow-up.

Botafogo 1967-70 (won the Carioca in his first season per FIFA), Flamengo, Fluminense, Vasco, Kuwait 1976-78, Al-Hilal, Saudi Arabia, UAE 1990 are excluded: none had tactical coverage in the sources found. Kuwait/UAE/Al-Hilal were only mentioned in passing; a later pass could test Botafogo 1967-70 (Saldanha-style 4-2-4 lineage) and UAE 1989-90.
The 1994 role under Parreira (World Cup win) is excluded as coordinator/assistant, not head coach. Single game in November 2002 (3-2 in South Korea, Wikipedia) excluded as too short.

sources.title: Mário Zagallo: The Tactical Masters - Coaches' Voice
sources.evidence: Ahead of Clodoaldo, the team's single pivot, Zagallo selected a group of five attacking players who constantly interchanged positions. (...) As a collective, Zagallo used his so-called ‘Five 10s’ (below) in a dynamic, fluid attacking structure.

sources.title: Mário Zagallo: Brazil's habitual World Cup winner
sources.evidence: The Seleção had qualified for the competition playing 4-2-4 – a formation Zagallo felt was out of date and would leave them exposed at a major international tournament. He would instead utilise a 4-3-3 – the same formation with which Brazil were victorious in 1958 – and brought the mesmerising talents of Rivellino into midfield.

sources.evidence: [Outside the counted spell (1995-98), kept as context] The next-generation Brazil team Zagallo brought to the 1998 World Cup in France utilised a defined 4-2-2-2 formation. (...) Unlike in 1970, however, Zagallo now turned to a double pivot in midfield. Dunga and César Sampaio were to provide defensive solidity in front of potentially exposed centre-backs.

sources.title: From beauty to beast: Brazil's transition from 1970 to 1974
sources.evidence: A heavily restructured squad, added to by Zagallo’s expectation for an overtly physical European show of intent, all meant that Brazil took a very different approach to the 1974 World Cup to the one they did in Mexico.

sources.title: Mário Zagallo: The Tactical Masters - Coaches' Voice
sources.evidence: Once Zagallo took over, however, he was moved back to play as a central defender. The idea was that Piazza's ability on the ball would improve the team’s build-up play from deep.

sources.title: Mário Zagallo: The Tactical Masters - Coaches' Voice
sources.evidence: [Outside the counted spell (1995-98), kept as context] Also unlike the 1970 team, Zagallo’s 1998 vintage started the build-up from the goalkeeper. Claudio Taffarel’s ability with the ball at his feet allowed him to find either centre-back – Aldair or Júnior Baiano – or one of the central midfielders with the first pass.

sources.title: Brazil, 1970 and the most beautiful football in history
sources.evidence: Zagallo expected the Italians to man-mark his players as the Uruguayans did before. To counter their measure, he instructed his men to keep possession and constantly pass the ball around to exhaust the Italians. It worked to perfection.

sources.title: Mário Zagallo: The Tactical Masters - Coaches' Voice

sources.title: Mário Zagallo: The Tactical Masters - Coaches' Voice

sources.title: Brazil, 1970 and the most beautiful football in history
sources.evidence: Brazil moved fast. They did not focus on hogging the ball nor defending deep.

sources.title: Mário Zagallo: The Tactical Masters - Coaches' Voice
sources.evidence: Zagallo also wanted to compress the pitch as much as possible in the defensive phase. When they progressed into the opponents’ half, a covering back line of three – both centre-backs and usually Everaldo, the less attacking full-back would push up as high as the halfway line.

sources.title: Mário Zagallo: The Tactical Masters - Coaches' Voice

The back four would start a few metres from the penalty area, with Gérson dropping alongside Clodoaldo into a midfield two ahead of them.

sources.title: Mário Zagallo: Brazil's habitual World Cup winner
sources.evidence: Zagallo took his team to Guanajuato for a 21-day training camp. The location was at a similar altitude to Mexico City where the World Cup final would be held. It played an important role in getting a team of undoubtedly gifted players into the best physical shape of their careers.

sources.title: From beauty to beast: Brazil's transition from 1970 to 1974
sources.evidence: Zagallo, despite being an attacking player himself, was a man who was inspired in a coaching capacity by the experiences of the man who entrusted him with a place in the Brazil side for the 1958 World Cup final. Vicente Feola would leave a lasting impact upon Zagallo, an impact which imparted to him just how important defensive cohesion was.

sources.title: A tribute to Mario Zagallo: 1931-2024 (FIFA)
sources.evidence: Just 75 days before the start of the FIFA World Cup 1970, Zagallo was put in charge of the Brazil team to replace João Saldanha, who led them through the qualifying campaign. Although there was little time to play with, Zagallo changed both the players and the system. “I had already formed the opinion that if Brazil took that (old) system to the World Cup, we wouldn’t get anywhere,” he told FIFA on his 90th birthday.
